conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , part of your surgical team. I understand you've been having a lot of pain in your left leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It’s been terrible—sharp, constant pain. I can’t even touch it without wincing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ve reviewed your history. You have severe peripheral vascular disease and diabetes, and the left leg has been affected by calciphylaxis and infection. The Achilles tendon is exposed and necrotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean? Is it worse now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, yes. The tissue is dying and infected. We believe the best option is to remove the affected part of your leg to stop the infection from spreading.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Amputation? You mean… cutting off my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re planning a below-knee amputation. It’s a two-step process. Tomorrow, we’ll do a guillotine amputation—removing the leg quickly to control the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once the infection is under control and swelling goes down, we’ll do a second surgery to reshape and close the stump properly. That’s called a re-amputation with closure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many surgeries… I’m scared it won’t heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your kidney transplant and diabetes do make healing harder. But leaving this infection untreated is much more dangerous. We’ll give you strong IV antibiotics starting today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… what antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole. They cover the most likely bacteria. Infectious disease helped us choose them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need blood transfusions again? Last time I felt so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low at 7.5, so we may need to give you blood before surgery. It helps your body handle the stress and improves healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my other medicines—my transplant drugs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll keep taking tacrolimus. The nephrology team is helping us manage your levels. We’ll check a level tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to lose the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. Your blood pressure has been fluctuating, so we’re adjusting your nifedipine and labetalol to protect your kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? The OxyContin isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted pain management. After surgery, you’ll get Dilaudid through a PCA pump—press a button when you need it. We’ll also start Lyrica to help with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake during the surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ll be under general anesthesia. We’ll also do a spinal block to help with pain afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished your pre-op chest X-ray. Lungs look clear, heart size normal. You’re good to go for surgery tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about my lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___ , you’re back from surgery. The guillotine amputation went well. We removed the infected part of your leg below the knee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How’s the wound? Is it… open?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we left it open for now to allow drainage and monitor for infection. We’ll close it in about three days once we’re sure things are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got two units before surgery. Your hematocrit went from 20 to 25.1. That’s a good improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain team adjusted your meds. You’re on Dilaudid PCA, Lyrica, and your usual OxyContin. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. The PCA helps a lot. But I’m a bit dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. We added baclofen yesterday for muscle spasms, but if it’s making you too sleepy, we can stop it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I can’t think straight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discontinue it. Your tacrolimus level was 4.3 this morning—on the low side—so we increased the dose to 4 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re monitoring closely. Your creatinine is stable at 1.4. That’s good for someone with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound looks clean—no signs of infection. We’re planning the second surgery—closure—tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re healing well. We’ll give you one unit of blood before surgery to boost your hemoglobin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery went well. We closed the stump and put in staples. The dressing is on now—we’ll remove it in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does it hurt more now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might feel tighter, but we’ve adjusted your pain meds. You’re now on oral Dilaudid as needed, plus acetaminophen and Lyrica.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We took the dressing off. The wound looks excellent—clean, dry, no redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I start moving around?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with help. You can sit in a wheelchair, but don’t put any weight on the stump. Physical therapy will help you learn to transfer safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my hand? The fingers are still black.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hand surgery saw you. The dry gangrene in your second and fourth fingers isn’t infected. No urgent surgery needed. You can follow up as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vancomycin trough was 18.6—good level. We’ll switch cipro and metronidazole to pills. Vancomycin will continue through your port for four more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll still get IV meds at the rehab center?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a nurse will give it daily. We’re also sending you with a clonidine patch for blood pressure and increasing your nifedipine to 90 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue glargine at bedtime and use sliding scale regular insulin as needed. Keep checking your sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow to an extended care facility for rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get a prosthesis someday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eventually, yes—but only after the wound fully heals, which takes at least four weeks. Staples stay in until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain? Will it ever go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should improve. We’re tapering the narcotics. Keep using Lyrica and acetaminophen. Let the rehab team know if pain flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to leave. Here’s your discharge plan—meds, wound care, and follow-up with vascular surgery in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’m nervous but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right path. Keep the stump elevated, clean, and dry. Call us if you see redness, drainage, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no one else removes the staples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Only your vascular surgeon decides when they come out. We’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. You’ve made great progress.
